judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: Logo in the InMobi/Quantcast consent dialog ('Take control of your privacy'). The crop shows the 'LeicestershireLive' wordmark, and the alt is 'Publisher Logo'. Read literally the claim is false: the image really is a publisher's logo. But the alt is generic placeholder text that leaves out what the logo conveys, the publisher's name (F30; logos take the organisation's name). The dialog's text names only 'Reach and across our entities', so the logo is its only mention of Leicestershire Live. Skeptic's checks: the page title names the site, but that does not make this alt an equivalent; and the logo is not decoration here. In good faith the claim ('describes something the image does not show' for an alt that leaves out what the image conveys) names the defect, as in the rubric's example. captureDiffers: the live CMP config (choice.js) sets displayUi 'always', the popup layout and the same publisherLogo URL (which returns 200), so users get this dialog and logo.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The image is all the header's Subscribe button holds. The crop shows the L logo plus 'SUBSCRIBE', and the alt 'leicestermercury' names the brand rather than the button's message, so the claim holds for the capture. But this non-text content is a control, and 1.1.1 asks only that the control have a name that describes its purpose. The link carries aria-label 'Subscribe to premium membership', which becomes its accessible name (the snapshot records nameFrom aria-label) and overrides the image's alt, so screen-reader users hear the right purpose. The visible 'Subscribe' also starts the name. Asking the inner alt to describe the picture is stricter than the criterion. captureDiffers: the button is rendered on the client (the server HTML has only its header container), and nothing suggests users get anything different from the snapshot.
